Topic Area 5 – Solvent Targeted Recovery and Precipitation (STRAP) of Plastic Wastes The most significant accomplishment of this project was the demonstration of the viability of STRAP to recover near-virgin quality polymer resins from a variety of plastic waste feedstocks. Initial studies (Walker et al, Sci Adv 2020) focused on the recovery of all polymer components of rigid, clear post-industrial multilayer plastic films and achieved >90% recoveries of pure resins (verified using FTIR) with properties (e.g., MFR) comparable to those of virgin resins. We found that using temperature-based precipitation, rather than antisolvent based precipitation, was effective and environmentally friendly, motivating a focus on temperature-based precipitation for further studies (Sanchez-Rivera et al, ChemSusChem, 2021). We successfully applied STRAP to recover resins for feedstocks of increasing complexity, including recovering PP from face masks (Yu et al, Green Chem 2023), recovering PE, EVOH, and PET from a reverse- printed multilayer plastic film (Sanchez-Rivera et al, Resourc Conserv Recycl 2023), recovering 10 distinct polymers from mixtures of post-industrial multilayer films (Sanchez- Rivera et al, Waste Manag 2025), and recovering polyolefins from municipal solid waste (Ra et al, Chem Eng J, submitted). We also demonstrated the recovery of high-quality polyethylene from post-consumer shrink wrap (Radkevich et al, Waste Manag, submitted). These examples highlight the versality of STRAP as a process to recover different types of resins from varied post-industrial and post-consumer feedstocks, including multilayer plastics for which there are no existing recycling technologies at scale. Importantly, STRAP consistently produces resins with near-virgin optical and mechanical properties with high purity and yield (>90%). The experimental accomplishments were enabled by advances in the computational modeling of polymer solubility as another key accomplishment of this project. The development of STRAP requires the selection of solvents and operating temperatures to ensure the selective dissolution and precipitation of target polymers from complex feedstocks. We developed thermodynamic modeling tools to predict temperature- dependent polymer solubilities (Zhou et al, ChemSusChem 2021), which we used to create a database with predicted solubilities of 11 polymers in 1000+ solvents (Zhou et al, Green Chem 2023). These tools were utilized in the development of the experimental STRAP processes described above. To analyze tradeoffs between solvent selection, process economics, and life cycle metrics, we developed computational tools to evaluate solvent “greenness” metrics as part of solvent selection (Ikegwu et al, Comput Chem Eng, 2025). These methods were incorporated as part of a framework to automatically enumerate all possible STRAP processes (with varying sequences of solvent washes and solvent selections) to identify tradeoffs between solvent selection both TEA/LCA metrics (Ikegwu et al, Comput Chem Eng, 2025). This suite of computational tools can help guide the development of STRAP processes for new feedstocks. Another significant accomplishment was the development of methods to scale-up STRAP to recover ~kg quantities of resins from multilayer films, enabling the production of cast films using industrial equipment in partnership with Amcor.
